game_title: Commanders of the Cosmos: Earth Climate Sentinel

questions.story: Welcome to Earth System Science Command! Your team is designing a satellite mission to measure changes in our planet's climate, oceans, and polar ice sheets.
questions.question: Which primary Earth observation orbit will you target?

source.title: NASA Earth Observatory Orbit Catalog
source.section: Orbital Selection for Earth Remote Sensing

answers.text: Target a 98.2° Sun-Synchronous Polar Orbit (SSO) at 700 km altitude.
answers.consequence_summary: Provides global polar-to-polar coverage with identical solar lighting on every pass, ideal for climate comparison.
answers.learning_point: Sun-synchronous orbits keep the Sun at the same angle relative to the ground, ensuring consistent shadows and lighting across years of imagery.

answers.text: Target an equatorial Low Earth Orbit (LEO) at 400 km altitude.
answers.consequence_summary: Saves launch delta-V and budget, but cannot view polar ice caps above 52° latitude.
answers.learning_point: Low inclination orbits require less launch rocket energy but miss high-latitude regions and polar ice entirely.

questions.story: In Sun-Synchronous orbit, your satellite flies over Greenland and Antarctica daily. Now you must choose the primary instrument to measure ice loss.
questions.question: Which remote-sensing instrument will you install?

source.title: NASA ICESat-2 Advanced Topographic Laser Altimeter System (ATLAS)
source.section: Laser Altimetry of Polar Ice Sheets

answers.consequence_summary: Measures ice sheet elevation changes down to 4 millimeters, detecting annual ice melt with unprecedented accuracy!
answers.learning_point: Photon-counting laser altimeters fire 10,000 laser pulses per second, timing individual photon reflections to map ice thickness.

answers.consequence_summary: Sees through polar cloud cover and winter darkness to track glacier flow speeds across Antarctica.
answers.learning_point: Radar waves penetrate cloud cover, smoke, and polar night, providing 24/7 all-weather surface deformation maps.

questions.story: From low equatorial orbit, your satellite frequently passes over tropical oceans and rainforests. Your team wants to study extreme weather and carbon cycles.
questions.question: Which payload configuration will you deploy?

source.title: NASA OCO-3 Greenhouse Gas Instrument Suite

answers.text: High-resolution Carbon Dioxide and Methane Spectrometer.
answers.consequence_summary: Detects greenhouse gas plumes over industrial centers and tropical wetlands with pinpoint precision.
answers.learning_point: Spectrometers measure narrow light absorption dips caused by CO2 molecules in the reflected sunlight column.

answers.text: Dual Optical Stereo Mapping Camera for disaster response.
answers.consequence_summary: Captures rapid-response 3D terrain maps of hurricane flooding and wildfire scars to aid rescue operations.
answers.learning_point: Stereo optical imaging provides actionable situational awareness during humanitarian and climate emergencies.

questions.story: Your photon-counting laser altimeter collects gigabytes of elevation profiles over the poles. You must transmit this massive data stream to ground stations.
questions.question: Which communications network will you use?

source.title: NASA Near Space Network (NSN) Polar Ground Stations

answers.text: Ka-band downlink to Svalbard and Fairbanks high-latitude ground stations.
answers.consequence_summary: Every polar pass downloads 100% of your laser altimetry data, delivering world-leading ice sheet melt models!
answers.learning_point: High-latitude ground stations in Norway and Alaska can see polar satellites on nearly every orbit (14 times per day).

answers.text: Standard S-band antenna downloading only to mid-latitude stations.
answers.consequence_summary: Limited contact times cause onboard memory to fill up, forcing instrument duty-cycling over Antarctica.
answers.learning_point: Without high-latitude ground stations, polar orbiters spend most of their flight out of direct contact with Earth.

questions.story: Your Synthetic Aperture Radar draws high electrical pulses (up to 800 Watts peak) during imaging bursts over glacier fronts.
questions.question: How will your power subsystem handle radar pulse demands?

answers.text: Install high-discharge-rate lithium battery banks paired with deployable solar wings.
answers.consequence_summary: Seamlessly buffers radar pulses, generating unbroken interferometric glacier deformation maps!
answers.learning_point: High-discharge batteries supply intense instantaneous current for radar bursts while solar wings recharge them steadily.

answers.text: Save mass by using small batteries, powering radar directly from solar panels.
answers.consequence_summary: Voltage drops sharply during a radar pulse in low-light conditions, tripping computer safe-mode brownouts.
answers.learning_point: Active sensors like radar require robust energy storage buffers to prevent bus voltage collapse.

questions.story: Your greenhouse gas spectrometer detects a sudden, massive methane spike over an offshore natural gas pipeline corridor.
questions.question: How will your mission control team respond?

source.title: NASA Earth Science Rapid Response System

answers.text: Slew the satellite to execute targeted point-source tracking and alert environmental agencies.
answers.consequence_summary: Confirms the exact pipeline rupture coordinates, allowing operators to shut the valve and prevent major emissions!
answers.learning_point: Agile pointing capabilities let Earth observatories pivot off-nadir to inspect urgent regional environmental anomalies.

answers.text: Maintain standard nadir pointing and catalog the data in the routine monthly archive.
answers.consequence_summary: Follows standard mission operations smoothly and provides dependable long-term atmospheric baselines.
answers.learning_point: Consistent nadir viewing provides unbroken statistical datasets for global climate modeling.

questions.story: During a category 5 hurricane landfall, coastal cellular towers collapse. First responders urgently need your satellite's flood extent imagery.
questions.question: Which dissemination protocol will you activate?

source.title: International Charter Space and Major Disasters

answers.text: Broadcast direct-to-ground open radio telemetry for immediate local antenna reception.
answers.consequence_summary: Delivers real-time flood maps directly to emergency rescue crews within 15 minutes of satellite overpass!
answers.learning_point: Direct broadcast systems bypass processing centers to beam imagery straight to handheld receivers in disaster zones.

answers.text: Route data through standard central processing servers for post-calibration.
answers.consequence_summary: Generates pristine, scientifically validated flood maps published 8 hours later.
answers.learning_point: Balancing speed versus scientific calibration is a key operational choice during disaster response.

endings.title: Gold-Standard Climate Observatory
endings.description: Outstanding achievement! Your Earth observation mission combined high-precision laser altimetry or radar sounding with polar Sun-Synchronous orbits and Ka-band downlinks. Scientists worldwide are citing your datasets in IPCC global climate assessments!
endings.scientific_explanation: Consistent sun-synchronous lighting and high-bandwidth polar ground station passes enabled continuous, uncompromised measurement of Earth's vital signs.
endings.learning_point: Long-term climate science requires stable orbits, high-precision sensors, and uninterrupted data downlinks.

endings.title: Dependable Earth System Monitor
endings.description: Mission success! Your satellite delivered steady, reliable environmental measurements while keeping launch costs low and battery margins wide.
endings.scientific_explanation: Conservative operational choices protected electrical systems and preserved spacecraft life for long-duration baseline monitoring.
endings.learning_point: In Earth remote sensing, maintaining an unbroken multi-year data record is often more valuable than high-risk experimental maneuvers.

endings.title: Heroic Rapid Disaster Response
endings.description: Life-saving performance! Your satellite provided critical real-time flood and storm imagery to first responders during climate emergencies.
endings.scientific_explanation: Direct broadcast and responsive targeting translated orbital technology into immediate humanitarian aid.
endings.learning_point: Space missions protect human lives on Earth by monitoring extreme weather and guiding evacuation operations.

endings.title: Constrained Data Return
endings.description: Satellite is healthy, but limited ground station visibility over the poles restricted data throughput, forcing instrument duty-cycling.
endings.scientific_explanation: Downlink bottlenecks prevent Earth orbiters from exploiting their sensors' full continuous mapping capabilities.
endings.learning_point: Ground station networks are an essential half of every Earth observation mission.

endings.title: Power Brownout Failure
endings.description: Spacecraft bus voltage collapsed! High radar power consumption overwhelmed the undersized battery during an eclipse pass, resetting flight computers.
endings.scientific_explanation: Pulse instruments require energy storage buffers to maintain steady computer voltage when solar generation drops.
endings.learning_point: Always size battery discharge capacity to handle peak payload demands, not just average power draw.
